hook.title: Tuning the radio dial
hook.text: Your data is a pile of signals; the parameter $\theta$ is a radio dial. At each dial position the model assigns some probability to *every* observation. The best dial position is the one under which your data is **least surprising**. Since each observation is independent, the probabilities **multiply**, and multiplying hundreds of tiny numbers is a nightmare, so we take the log and the product becomes a **sum**. But beware: a dial tuned so tightly to *these* signals that it fails on *new* ones hasn't learnt anything.
hook.recall: Remember the radio dial: log turns the product of independent likelihoods into a sum without moving the best dial position. And a great fit to old data says nothing about unseen signals.

explore.intro: Two tabs: the likelihood landscape, and fit-versus-generalise.
tasks: Coin tab: observe 7 heads in 10 flips. Where does the curve peak? Add more flips with the same proportion: does the peak move? Does the curve get sharper?
Fit tab: slide the model width $h$ down to near zero. Watch train vs test log-likelihood.
explore.takeaway: MLE: $\theta^*=\arg\max_\theta\sum_n\log p(x_n;\theta)$ under i.i.d. A model should be judged by test data, because training fit alone can be inflated.

items: Assume the $x_n$ are i.i.d. so $p(D;\theta)=\prod_n p(x_n;\theta)$
Check the fit on held-out data (generalisation)
build.explanation: Slide 19 states the objective and the i.i.d. step; slide 20 says generalisation (test-data performance) is the key factor.

questions.prompt: Why do we maximise $\sum_n\log p(x_n;\theta)$ rather than $\prod_n p(x_n;\theta)$?
options: The log changes which $\theta$ is best
Under the i.i.d. assumption the product becomes a sum, which is easier to work with, and the maximiser stays the same
The product is always larger than the sum
The log makes probabilities bigger than 1
questions.explanation: The dial position that makes the data least surprising doesn’t change when you take logs. Log is increasing. It just converts the product to a sum.

questions.prompt: 10 coin flips gave 7 heads. The Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate of $\theta=P(\text{heads})$ is:
questions.explanation: Maximising $k\log\theta+(n-k)\log(1-\theta)$ gives $\theta^*=k/n=0.7$. (Closed-form Bernoulli MLE is standard textbook context, not stated on the slides; the explorer shows it visually.)

options: A simple strategy is to maximise the log-likelihood
A model that fits the training set perfectly always generalises best
questions.explanation: A dial tuned to memorise old signals can assign almost no probability to new ones. The slides say generalisation capability, i.e. test-data performance, is the key factor.

questions.prompt: Three i.i.d. observations have $p(x_1)=0.5$, $p(x_2)=0.2$, $p(x_3)=0.1$ under some model. What is $p(x_1,x_2,x_3)$?
questions.explanation: i.i.d. ⇒ the joint is the product: $0.5\times0.2\times0.1=0.01$. (Its log is a sum of three logs.)

questions.prompt: *“My model’s training log-likelihood is higher than my friend’s, so my model is better.”* What is the flaw?
options: None: higher likelihood always means better
Training likelihood doesn’t measure generalisation. Compare on held-out/test data
Log-likelihood can only be compared on the test set of the other person
Higher likelihood means a worse model
questions.explanation: A tight dial can ace the signals it memorised and fail on fresh ones, exactly what the Fit tab’s tiny-width model does.
